items.title: Coding gives you a window into what the future will look like for a large amount…
items.summaryText:
Coding gives you a window into what the future will look like for a large amount of knowledge work. 

The first step for most jobs is that we go from doing most of the research, typing, and value creation manually (even if it’s using digital tools) to soon coordinating the work that agents are doing. 

Next, as this step itself becomes redundant or slows down what agents are capable of, we will be giving agents goals to optimize against and they’ll go off on and increasingly solve larger problems for us. 

This may at first blush look like something whose impact gets stuck with coding, but actually a large percentage of knowledge work may eventually just converge with this form factor due to the massive productivity gains that can be generated. Agents will use computers, leverage our existing tools or write new ones, and write code on the fly to solve larger swaths of knowledge work. 

So even if a task today doesn’t seem to be “coding” directly, the task may eventually fold into being coding adjacent. Manufacturing, architecture, life sciences, material sciences, cyber, and on and on.
 
One big hurdle in the way ultimately will be that much of this work remains non-verifiable, so humans will be even more in the loop than they are in coding. But the part that they can hand off will just get bigger and bigger over time as the models are more capable.

So in short, pay attention to coding and you’ll get a sense for where work is going.

metadata.bio: ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI

items.summaryZh:
编程为你打开一扇窗，让你看到大量知识工作未来的样子。

对大多数工作来说，第一步是从我们亲手完成大部分研究、打字和价值创造（即便使用的是数字工具），很快转变为协调智能体所做的工作。

接下来，当这一步本身变得多余，或拖慢智能体能力时，我们就会给智能体设定要优化的目标，它们会自行出发，越来越多地替我们解决更大的问题。

乍看之下，这似乎只是影响局限在编程领域的事，但实际上，由于可能带来巨大的生产力提升，很大一部分知识工作最终或许会收敛到这种形态。智能体会使用计算机，利用我们现有的工具或编写新工具，并即时编写代码，以解决更大范围的知识工作。

所以，即使今天某项任务看起来并不直接是“编程”，这项任务最终也可能并入与编程相邻的范畴。制造业、建筑业、生命科学、材料科学、网络安全，等等，不一而足。

最终的一大障碍将是，这类工作中的许多仍然无法验证，因此人类在其中的参与会比在编程中更多。但随着模型能力越来越强，他们能交出去的部分只会随着时间推移越来越大。

简而言之，关注编程，你就能感知工作将走向何方。

items.title: I asked Claude to populate a Civilization-style game map with real data from the…
items.summaryText:
I asked Claude to populate a Civilization-style game map with real data from the US. Opus 5.5 downloaded and parse a ton of public data and 7 hours and 45K lines of code later... it works :)

- 31 real data sources including Census, BEA, BLS, EIA, NOAA, USGS, DoD, NPS, FAA, FEMA, CDC...
- Real elevation, land cover, GDP, jobs, power plants, mines, ports, airports, bases, parks, universities, freight flows, disasters; all reconciled onto one 25 km hex grid.
- The data is converted into Civilization language, e.g. Gold yield is GDP. A city's districts are its real industry specializations: San Jose gets a Campus, Detroit is "Motor city". Its citizens are its real workforce: 1 in 4 San Jose workers are engineers, coders or scientists, against 1 in 14 nationally. Wonders are chosen by published rules, such as national parks by visitor numbers and universities by R&D spending, etc etc.
- 19 lenses (income, degrees, faith, disasters…), a City View for 524 metros, and nine advisors plus an Explorer. The Explorer turns any column for any of 3,100+ counties into a table and scatter plot, linked to the map.
- Claude decided to skip a few states and territories sry
- Built using Claude Code desktop app, Opus 5.5 on medium and turning on ultracode.

It's deployed here: https://t.co/QMhmafXMj5 and the "?" has the source link too. I don't exactly know where I was going with this but it's really fun to browse and play with. Possibly it can be expanded or built into a game. I only have half of my weekly Claude quote left though so someone else will have to take over :D. Claude also made a trailer:

items.title: AI native teams will eventually force the surrounding organization to become AI…
items.summaryText:
AI native teams will eventually force the surrounding organization to become AI native too.

Take software development. coding velocity is way up thanks to AI, while actual shipped products and business impact are unchanged in most companies. That’s cos the surrounding system of experimentation tooling, evaluation, launch processes, and gtm are outdated.

It’s like sticking a Ferrari engine in a sedan and racing it on Indian roads. The engine can rev faster but the car speed is limited by its system and environment.

AI native companies were built ground up for this new way of building and shipping. They’re also able to shed suboptimal processes faster.

Market forces will quickly force all companies to adapt or perish.

If you’re solving this for your company: map out your product lifecycle and rebuild it ground up - tooling, team structure, gtm, everything.

items.title: OpenAI’s Noam Brown: Why Game Theory Didn’t Lead to General Intelligence (Live at No Limit Finals)
items.summaryText:
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:22
Please join me in a round of applause for Noam and Alfred. Hey, Noam. Thank you for coming. It's been a rainy day, and this is this is actually all because of you, because you started studying poker for a while. You and I talked a little bit about your r…
items.bodyText:
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:22
Please join me in a round of applause for Noam and Alfred. Hey, Noam. Thank you for coming. It's been a rainy day, and this is this is actually all because of you, because you started studying poker for a while. You and I talked a little bit about your research before you went to OpenAI.

Speaker 1 | 00:22 - 00:35
You went from studying poker to studying game theory and diplomacy to now reasoning. Like, what... Tell us about... A little bit about your path. Why did you decide to study poker of all all things?

Speaker 2 | 00:35 - 00:44
Yeah. So first of it's great to be here. It's really exciting to see all these people working, like, able to do so much in an hour. I'm I'm... I think it's really incredible.

Speaker 2 | 00:46 - 01:04
My journey, I started... I finished undergrad. I wasn't really sure what I wanted to do, and I figured I wanted to do research. And I wasn't really sure in what. And when I was looking at grad schools, there was this professor that was looking for people to work on AI to play poker, and I thought this is great.

Speaker 2 | 01:04 - 01:26
I have a lot of interest in game theory. I have a lot of interest in computer science, economics, and I had played poker a lot in high school and college, and I loved the game. And I thought it was always really fascinating that there was this perfect strategy to poker that nobody... And nobody knew what it was. But if you could find it, you could just make unlimited money.

Speaker 2 | 01:26 - 01:37
So I started working on that basically as soon as I started grad school in 2012 and worked on it continuously through my whole PhD. And it's actually pretty unusual to to work on something.

Speaker 1 | 01:37 - 01:39
Money during that time too?

Speaker 2 | 01:39 - 02:04
I never used it to play online poker, but there is a fun fact. There was the precursor to this, I guess, the MIT PokerBots competition, which ran for several years. And as a poor grad student, I wanted to enter this competition because there was 10,000 in prize money. And I wasn't at MIT, so I got one of my MIT friends to collaborate collaborate with me, and we submitted the poker bot. We won two years in a row, 2014 and 2015.

Speaker 2 | 02:04 - 02:11
And after that, I kinda felt bad about, you know, beating up all these people that don't really know how big poker bots, so I stopped doing it after that.

Speaker 1 | 02:12 - 02:19
Did you... So if you had sixty minutes to go build a poker bot today, given all that you know, how would you start? It's a

Speaker 2 | 02:19 - 02:38
great question. I'm actually curious to talk to the contestants in here, what strategies they took. The the approaches that we took were very GTO based. And so we would have the agents running, but we basically have the model training, playing self... Do it through self play using CFR.

Speaker 2 | 02:39 - 03:17
Later on, it turned into these more neural net based self play approaches, but everything was focused on self play to converge to GTO. And the problem there is that it takes a long time to train. The coding part you can do without modern LMs, I think you could make the code to run that in an hour, but the training process itself could take many hours. I think you could make a pretty low fidelity GTO bot in an hour. I think if you did k means clustering to reduce the abstraction size to, like, a pretty small, size and then did self play for, like, let's say, thirty minutes, you could actually probably get a a half decent poker bot.

Speaker 2 | 03:19 - 03:52
That said, the format, because it's multiplayer and because you're not doing, like, an instant runoff kind of tournament where you're always going to, like, eliminate the weakest competitors, but you're actually playing against all the competitors, I could see an exploitation based approach actually being the better one for this kind of tournament structure. So I think in this setup, I would probably go for an exploitation based approach and try to find the... You know, try to observe the weaknesses of the opponents and then exploit that, especially in a multi a multi handed... Multiplayer situation.

Speaker 1 | 03:52 - 04:05
You're gonna have to submit your own code next year. We're gonna have to have you compete, but you can't win. So I think you make more... You make enough at OpenAI, hopefully. Because the prize money is only a $100,000.

Speaker 1 | 04:05 - 04:07
Hopefully, they pay you a little bit more than that.

Speaker 2 | 04:07 - 04:28
The other thing I'd be curious to see is how well the LLMs do playing in in this tournament. So not not just using it to make a poker bot, but if you play the poker bots against, let's say, GPT six Astra, how Astra would do. Because we've been tracking the performance of... Like, I've been tracking the performance of the... Of these different general purpose LLMs over time.

Speaker 2 | 04:28 - 04:37
And with Astra, like, with... As recent models have developed, they've actually gotten quite good. And Astra, I would say, is actually, like, able to make money playing online poker at this point.

Speaker 1 | 04:37 - 05:02
Yeah. So maybe back up a step because you you obviously went from poker to diplomacy to reasoning, and now these can do a lot more than just play poker and do it extremely well. Take us through your journey of, like, how you, like, let... Took your learnings from poker to diplomacy, game theory around diplomacy to then... Into reasoning.

Speaker 1 | 05:02 - 05:04
I think that's a really interesting path.

Speaker 2 | 05:04 - 05:20
Yeah. The original motivation for working on poker was that there had been a lot of progress on Go and Go and chess, you know, perfect information games. And the problem is that if you only have a technique that works on a very narrow domain, then it's actually not that useful. Right? Because you you want something that's general purpose.

Speaker 2 | 05:20 - 05:53
And so the motivation for working on poker was that we can figure out new things about what techniques actually work on these... In these other domains and and eventually make this more general purpose AI that can, for example, play both Go and poker. And after we made the poker bots, I think we did actually learn quite a bit, but the truth is that they weren't that good for chess or Go. And so I wanted to, like, try something more ambitious, something that would expand the the scope of of of games that these techniques would be able to play. And at the time, it was around 2019, g p d z...

Speaker 2 | 05:53 - 06:08
G p d two had come out, and it started to look like there would be rapid progress in language models. And I thought, like... I I honestly, like, our our... The original thing that I was discussing with my teammates was, oh, we we wanna wanna... We wanna make an AI that could play both Go and poker.

Speaker 2 | 06:08 - 06:42
But considering how rapid progress in AI was in 2019, we thought that wouldn't be ambitious enough. And so we wanted to target the game that we thought would be the hardest to make an AI for, which we felt was diplomacy because it is a natural language game that involves negotiations with other players, because it's not just purely adversarial, it's also cooperative, you have to form alliances. In 2019, it was unthinkable that you could have an AI play this game well. And we thought, like, that's that's the perfect thing to aim for. Poker took decades for people to work on.

Speaker 2 | 06:42 - 07:01
If if we have to spend, like, five years making an AI that could finally play diplomacy, that's that's great. So we took it on, and and we learned a lot along the way. And and one of the things that I took away is that, actually, the the game theory approach doesn't actually work that well in diplomacy. Like, I originally came

Speaker 1 | 07:01 - 07:12
in Say say say more about that because I I thought that game theory was developed to actually be a much better negotiator in a repeat game and and and especially in diplomacy.

Speaker 2 | 07:12 - 07:40
I I think there is intuition that you can take away from game theory, but the problem with game theory is that it assumes... This is the the central premise of game theory that it assumes that all the other players are rational, that it is common knowledge that all players are rational, and people are not actually rational. And if you come in with this assumption and you make it a central pillar that everybody's rational, then you're going to do... You're gonna make mistakes. And so I think, like, a a good example is, are you familiar with the ultimatum game?

Speaker 1 | 07:40 - 07:41
Well, you should explain Yeah.

Speaker 2 | 07:41 - 07:53
So it's this idea that there's two players, Alice and Bob. Alice has a $100. They can offer Bob anywhere between 0 and a $100. And Bob can, can either accept or reject. And if Bob rejects, they both get zero.

Speaker 2 | 07:53 - 08:08
If Bob accepts, then they split the money that way. So if Alice were to offer Bob $10 and Bob accepts, then Alice gets 90, Bob gets 10. And the game theory optimal approach for this game is to just offer Bob like a penny. Yeah.

Speaker 1 | 08:09 - 08:11
Some small amount. Yes.

Speaker 2 | 08:11 - 08:19
The small amount. Yeah. And if you... And and, you know, like, this makes sense. You you know, Bob Bob has a choice between making a penny or making zero, like, the penny's worth more.

Speaker 2 | 08:19 - 08:28
But, But, I mean, you can imagine what would happen if you actually tried to offer somebody a penny in this game. Like, of course, they would say... Yeah. They would say no. What we found is that our poker...

Speaker 2 | 08:28 - 09:02
That that our diplomacy bots, when we took this very game theory approach, would start doing these kinds of behaviors. And there's like this temptation to say, oh, we we can try to find... We can try to encode some semblance, some like notion of of vengeance or or fairness into the into the bots. And when you go down this rabbit hole, eventually, what we realized is that actually it's too nuanced. And the real way to make a superhuman diplomacy AI is to train on human data, to just understand people to such an...

Speaker 2 | 09:03 - 09:18
Yeah. To not take a game theoretic approach. Do not assume rationality, but to just assume that people are gonna behave like people, understand what that means by training on a lot of human data, and and then determine what what is my best course of action given the behaviors of everybody else.

Speaker 1 | 09:18 - 09:24
And so do you end up with a model of human irrationality then? That's the idea, that you end up with

Speaker 2 | 09:24 - 09:39
a model of human irrationality. So we train these models that their purpose is to imitate people as closely as possible. And then we train the AI with these imitation humans and do a lot of do a lot of training, and then we can deploy that in the real world with actual humans. And that... That's what does best.

Speaker 1 | 09:39 - 10:08
There's a book by two behavioral economists about thinking fast and slow. And a lot of that has to do with... Kahneman just explains, like, there are signs of, like, consistent bugs in our brains. And we we sort of have these solutions that are imperfect. And you can explain why it happens from behavioral economics point of view, but it isn't the rational reasoned approach.

Speaker 1 | 10:10 - 10:15
How have you sort of incorporated that into, like, reasoning and and doing research and reasoning at OpenAI?

Speaker 2 | 10:16 - 10:49
Yeah. So after the diplomacy results, I had an interesting choice in my career at that point because this was around 2022. I think around early twenty twenty two, it was becoming clear that the game theory approach, it was not working in diplomacy and actually that the right approach was this kind of like more modeling of human behavior. And this was kind of like a crisis of faith moment for me because my entire career up until that point had been about game theory. By area, it was computational game theory, my expertise was computational game theory.

Speaker 2 | 10:49 - 11:36
And I had to wrestle with the fact that actually that was not the path to general intelligence, that actually if you look at the evidence, it was this training on a lot of human data, modeling people really well, and then teaching the model to interact with that environment, and then also the scaling up of reasoning thing. And so I had to choose between like, okay, well, do I stick with computational game theory despite me thinking that this is not the most important direction, the most promising path to general intelligence? Or do I pivot and do I work on what I think is actually the the the most valuable thing despite it not being my... You know, what what I'm an expert at, which is general purpose reasoning in RL. And I ultimately decided to go the path of what I felt was most impactful, which was actually just pivot and work on this general reasoning direction.

Speaker 2 | 11:37 - 11:52
And so this led me to join OpenAI. I looked at a lot of different places, and I told them, like, what I wanna work on, these LLMs, they're really cool. They're really general, but they can't play Go. They can't play poker. Why not?

Speaker 2 | 11:52 - 12:13
And at the time, was a very... It's hard to put yourself in like 2022, I guess. Maybe people will remember what it was like back then, but people were extremely bullish on just scaling up pre training. And I would go to some places and I would say like, look, reasoning is gonna be this essential ingredient. And people would tell me like, well, actually we should just pre train a bigger model and that'll solve all the problems.

Speaker 2 | 12:14 - 12:35
And if we get to... And yeah, GPT-four can't play Go, it sucks at chess, it sucks at poker, but we just do like a few more orders of magnitude of training, maybe it'll just work. And I would point to the evidence and say, like, actually, no. If you look at how much you would have to skill it up by for a game like... To to be able to play Go competently, it would be about, like, six orders of magnitude.

Speaker 2 | 12:35 - 12:52
And that doesn't seem, you know, realistic. And, fortunately, OpenAI was actually really bullish about this direction. So... And I didn't know this at time, but they actually had a team working on on this on this direction of how do you get general purpose reasoning out of these language models. And so ultimately, I joined OpenAI.

Speaker 2 | 12:52 - 12:59
It works on what became o one. And... Yeah, and now these models, like, they can play these games extremely well. It's just general

Speaker 1 | 12:59 - 13:09
purpose. Changed over the last few years? What was it that breakthroughs that allow them to... As you said, it's not just scaling it up. So what were the major breakthroughs along the way?

Speaker 2 | 13:10 - 13:36
I think the major takeaway from my work on poker, diplomacy, and then also looking back at games like backgammon and chess was that you needed these AIs to think before acting. So when I started working on poker bots in 2012 and 2013, there was no reasoning going into these models. They would just act instantly. And there were a lot of reasons for this. A big factor is actually the structure of the tournaments, this this tournament included, is that it doesn't really give you much time.

Speaker 2 | 13:36 - 14:13
It doesn't give the the the model much time to actually reason before it has to act. It's a very short clock and that's kind of like essential because poker is a high variance game and so you need to play a lot of hands and so you can't have it sit there for ten seconds thinking for every single hand. But people do that, right? People, if they're faced with a tough decision, will think through their decisions that they have to make And that obviously benefits them instead of having to act instantly. So seeing this general trend of like, okay, in all of these games, chess, go, poker, diplomacy, we had to have these AIs think very carefully before acting in order to beat top humans.

Speaker 2 | 14:13 - 14:42
How do we get this out of LLMs? And at the time, there was chain of thought, which is the idea that you just prompt the model and say, think step by step before answering. And there was some evidence that this actually led to better solutions, but it was very coarse. It was not really sophisticated. And it turned out the key ingredient was, yeah, if you do reinforcement learning to train for this behavior, then you actually get much better chain of thought behavior, you get much better outputs.

Speaker 2 | 14:42 - 14:59
And then also what we observe at that point is actually the longer the model takes to think before responding, the better it does. And that that was, I think, the key unlock that was like, okay. Now we have a way to scale up test time compute, not just in these games, but actually in a general purpose way with language models that can be applied to basically any domain.

Speaker 1 | 14:59 - 15:14
Great. I have a few more questions, but, hey, start thinking about what you would like to ask now because we're gonna open up for q and a. I think a lot of people here are incredible. They're... You know, like, the people here were smarter when I was in college.

Speaker 1 | 15:16 - 15:36
They're all very mathy people, very AI pill people. They're probably all very AI... AJI pill people as well. But OpenAI keeps solving math problem after math problem after math problem, very complicated ones. So what would you recommend people here do so that they are not left behind?

Speaker 1 | 15:36 - 15:47
